warmup.q: Inside customer { } of an order-form DSL with no @DslMarker, someone writes deliverTo { name = "oops" } by mistake. What happens?
options: It doesn't compile: deliverTo isn't a member of ContactBuilder
It compiles and calls deliverTo on the outer OrderFormBuilder
It compiles and builds an address nested inside the customer
It compiles and is ignored at run time
warmup.why: Both receivers are in scope inside customer { }, and Kotlin tries an unqualified call against each of them, nearest first. ContactBuilder has no deliverTo, so the outer builder's deliverTo is used. The first option is what most people expect, which is exactly why the bug survives review. The third section shows the run and the fix, @DslMarker.

opening:
Every order at the print shop starts on a paper form. It has a section for the customer, a section for the delivery address and a box for the number of copies. Each section offers only its own boxes, so nobody writes a phone number where the copies should go.

Kotlin lets you write such a form as code: a DSL, a domain-specific language made for one job. Each section becomes a block in braces, and inside a block you fill in boxes by name. The trick is a lambda that runs inside an object. The surprise is a box the section doesn't have. Kotlin quietly looks in the sections around it and fills in the first box with that name. It compiles. It even runs, for a while.

In the last lesson, by made the compiler write forwarding code for us. This time we design the words ourselves, and the compiler checks every sentence. We'll see what a lambda with a receiver is on the JVM, build a booklet order from builder classes, close the trap with @DslMarker and call it all from Java. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with the shop's order form, where each section offers only its own boxes. A lambda with a receiver is one section clipped to a clipboard, builder classes are the sections, and @DslMarker stops a missing box from falling through to the section around it.

In your own code, find a DSL with nested blocks and write one call in the wrong block on purpose. If it compiles, the builders need a marker.

Next, we'll meet context parameters, the replacement for context receivers, and contracts, which tell the compiler facts it can't work out alone. How can your own check function make a nullable value safe to use on the next line, the way require does?

sections.h: A lambda with a receiver: code that runs inside an object
sections.html:
Start with something every Java programmer has written: a StringBuilder that builds a line of text, one append at a time. The print shop's app makes job tickets this way, little slips such as flyer.pdf x 250 that go into each job's folder. Here is a helper that makes one, in both languages:

Java
// Java has no receiver lambdas. Its idiom: a Consumer that receives the builder as a parameter.
static String ticket(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    block.accept(sb);
    return sb.toString();
}

ticket(sb -> sb.append("flyer.pdf x ").append(250));
Kotlin
fun ticket(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString()

ticket { append("flyer.pdf x "); append(250) }    // `this` is the StringBuilder

The part in braces is a lambda, a small function written in place and passed as a value. The two calls look almost the same, but one thing is missing in the Kotlin one: the sb.. Inside its braces, append is called on the builder without naming it.

The object a call is made on is the call's receiver. In sb.append(x), the receiver is sb. Inside a class's own methods the receiver is this, and you usually leave it out. That's why a method of StringBuilder can call append with no prefix.

The parameter type in the Kotlin version, StringBuilder.() -> Unit, is a function type with a receiver. A lambda of that type runs with a StringBuilder as its this, so inside its braces you write code as if you were writing a method of StringBuilder. In the print shop, it's a clerk handed a form already clipped to a clipboard. She writes in the boxes without saying which form, because she's holding it. apply, with and run from the standard library are all built on this one idea.

You may wonder what the JVM makes of it. The JVM has no idea what a receiver is. To the JVM, StringBuilder.() -> Unit and (StringBuilder) -> Unit are one and the same: kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<StringBuilder, Unit>, Kotlin's interface for a function with one parameter. The receiver is simply the first argument. So Kotlin lets you assign one type to the other, and it lets you call a receiver lambda both ways, sb.withReceiver() or withReceiver(sb). Only the compiler cares about the difference, because it decides what this means inside the braces.

That is also exactly what Java sees. Java calls the Kotlin ticket with a lambda that gets the builder as a parameter, and the lambda has to end with return Unit.INSTANCE. A Kotlin function with nothing useful to return returns Unit, and to Java, Unit is a real object. Leave the line out, and javac, the Java compiler, says bad return type in lambda expression and missing return value. It's a small toll Java pays on every block.

Two more facts turn this into a language. A receiver lambda can take ordinary parameters too: Builder.(Int) -> Unit gets a this and an Int. And an extension function, a function you declare as if it were a member of a class you didn't write, works like a named lambda with receiver. A fun BookletBuilder.folded(...) can be called inside any BookletBuilder.() -> Unit block. The worked example uses that to add a new word to the shop's DSL.

A lambda with a receiver is a lambda whose first parameter is this. Inside its braces, you call the receiver's members by name.

One clipboard holds one form. A real order has sections inside sections, and for that we need builders.

try.title: Call a receiver lambda both ways
steps: In ReceiverDemo.kt, try the reverse assignment: val back: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = withReceiver. Predict whether it compiles, then run.
In the Java twin, delete return Unit.INSTANCE; from the first lambda and run. Read javac's complaint.

code.title: ReceiverDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo // Two function types. Inside the first, the StringBuilder is `this`; in the second it's a parameter. val withReceiver: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = { append("copies: "); append(250) } val withParameter: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = { sb -> sb.append("copies: ").append(250) } /** An ordinary function that takes a lambda with receiver: the smallest possible DSL entry point. */ fun ticket(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString() fun main() { val sb = StringBuilder() sb.withReceiver() // call it like an extension function... withReceiver(sb) // ...or pass the receiver as the first argument println(sb) val swapped: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = withParameter // the two types are interchangeable println(ticket(swapped)) println(ticket { append("flyer.pdf x "); append(250) }) println("JVM type of withReceiver: ${withReceiver.javaClass.interfaces.joinToString { it.name }}") }

alt.title: ReceiverDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import kotlin.Unit; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * Java twin of ReceiverDemo.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers. A Kotlin * StringBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<StringBuilder, Unit> to Java: the receiver is the first parameter. */ public class ReceiverDemoJava { // Java's own idiom for the same job: a Consumer that gets the builder as a parameter static String ticketJava(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); block.accept(sb); return sb.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { String t = ReceiverDemoKt.ticket(sb -> { sb.append("flyer.pdf x ").append(250); return Unit.INSTANCE; // Kotlin's Unit is a real object here }); System.out.println(t); System.out.println(ticketJava(sb -> sb.append("menu.pdf x ").append(40))); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); ReceiverDemoKt.getWithReceiver().invoke(sb); // a receiver lambda, invoked with the receiver as argument System.out.println(sb); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints copies: 250copies: 250 (one call as an extension, one with the receiver as an argument), then copies: 250, flyer.pdf x 250 and JVM type of withReceiver: kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1. The reverse assignment compiles too. Without return Unit.INSTANCE, javac stops with incompatible types: bad return type in lambda expression and missing return value: Function1.invoke returns an object, so a Java lambda for it has to return something.

sections.h: Builder classes and an entry function: a booklet order in a few lines
sections.html:
Every section of an order needs its own clipboard, and some sections hold smaller ones. Take a booklet, such as a restaurant menu: a cover on thick card, then a few parts on plain paper, say the starters and the mains. The shop makes booklets by folding sheets in half, and one folded sheet gives four pages. So every booklet needs a multiple of 4 pages, or a customer gets blank pages nobody asked for.

The pattern Kotlin's docs call a type-safe builder has two pieces. A builder class holds the state and offers the words: properties to set and functions to call. An entry function creates the builder, runs your lambda on it, and returns the finished result. Here is the lab's booklet builder, cut down to its shape:

Java
// Java: the builder arrives as a parameter, and every line names it
static Booklet printBooklet(String title, Consumer<BookletBuilder> block) {
    BookletBuilder b = new BookletBuilder(title);
    block.accept(b);
    return b.build();
}

Booklet menu = printBooklet("menu", b -> {
    b.setNote("staple on the fold");
    b.cover(4);
    b.pages("starters", 4);
    b.pages("mains", 8);
});
Kotlin
class BookletBuilder(private val title: String) {
    var note = ""
    private val parts = mutableListOf<Part>()

    fun cover(pages: Int) = add("cover", Paper.CARD, pages)
    fun pages(name: String, pages: Int) = add(name, Paper.PLAIN, pages)
    private fun add(name: String, paper: Paper, pages: Int) { /* checks pages > 0, then adds a Part */ }

    fun build(): Booklet { /* checks the whole booklet, returns a copy of the parts */ }
}

fun printBooklet(title: String, block: BookletBuilder.() -> Unit): Booklet =
    BookletBuilder(title).apply(block).build()

val menu = printBooklet("menu") {
    note = "staple on the fold"
    cover(4)
    pages("starters", 4)
    pages("mains", 8)
}

The Kotlin entry function is one line, BookletBuilder(title).apply(block).build(). It creates a builder, runs the block with that builder as this, and turns the builder into a finished Booklet. The Java version does the same three steps by hand, and its block names the builder, b., on every line.

Nesting is the same trick again. The lab's OrderBuilder has a function booklet(title) { ... } that takes another receiver lambda, so an order holds booklets the way a form holds sections. No library is involved: only classes, functions and lambdas with receivers.

Where does checking go? Check a single bad value at the call that passes it, so the error points at the wrong line: pages("mains", -4) fails inside pages. Check rules that span several calls in build(), the one place that sees the whole booklet. In the lab, a 4-page cover and a 10-page concert programme make 14 pages, and build() turns it away with booklet programme has 14 pages: a folded booklet needs a multiple of 4.

Check one value where it's passed, and the rules between values in build().

The standard library ships three builders of its own that you can use today:

Java
List<Line> building = new ArrayList<>();
building.add(new Line("flyer.pdf", 250, 1));
building.add(new Line("menu.pdf", 40, 8));
if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new Line("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1));
List<Line> lines = List.copyOf(building);              // freeze it with a copy

String text = new StringBuilder().append("pages to print=").append(571).toString();
Kotlin
val lines = buildList {
    add(Line("flyer.pdf", 250, 1))
    add(Line("menu.pdf", 40, 8))
    if (size == 2) add(Line("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1))   // `this` is a MutableList
}
val printed = buildMap { for (l in lines) put(l.file, l.copies * l.pages) }
val text = buildString { append("pages to print="); append(printed.values.sum()) }

Inside buildList { }, this is a MutableList, so add, addAll and even size work. The result is typed List, and it really is read-only. The demo casts it back to MutableList, calls add, and gets an UnsupportedOperationException. That's what you want from a builder: changeable while you build, fixed once you're done. Java gets the same result with List.copyOf, at the price of one copy.

buildList, buildMap and buildString are inline, so their lambdas cost nothing at run time (lesson 1 of this track). Your own entry functions can be inline too, though they usually run a few times per order, so it rarely matters.

Builders nest nicely. They also nest a little too nicely, and that is where a bug can hide.

try.title: Use the standard builders
steps: Run BuildersDemo and BuildersDemoJava. They print the same four lines.
In buildList { }, add println(this::class.simpleName) as the first line. Predict whether you'll see ArrayList, then run.
Move the if (size == 2) line above the two add calls and run again. What changed, and why?

code.title: BuildersDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo data class Line(val file: String, val copies: Int, val pages: Int) fun main() { val lines = buildList { add(Line("flyer.pdf", 250, 1)) add(Line("menu.pdf", 40, 8)) if (size == 2) add(Line("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1)) // `this` is a MutableList, so size works here } val printed = buildMap { for (l in lines) put(l.file, l.copies * l.pages) } val text = buildString { append("pages to print=") append(printed.values.sum()) } println(lines.map { it.file }) println(printed) println(text) try { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") (lines as MutableList<Line>).add(Line("late.pdf", 1, 1)) } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println("the built list is read-only: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } }

alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Java twin of BuildersDemo.kt. Java builds a mutable collection, then copies it into an * unmodifiable one. buildList and buildString are inline-only Kotlin functions, so Java can't call them. */ public class BuildersDemoJava { record LineJava(String file, int copies, int pages) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<LineJava> building = new ArrayList<>(); building.add(new LineJava("flyer.pdf", 250, 1)); building.add(new LineJava("menu.pdf", 40, 8)); if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new LineJava("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1)); List<LineJava> lines = List.copyOf(building); Map<String, Integer> printed = new LinkedHashMap<>(); for (LineJava l : lines) printed.put(l.file(), l.copies() * l.pages()); String text = new StringBuilder() .append("pages to print=") .append(printed.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum()) .toString(); System.out.println(lines.stream().map(LineJava::file).toList()); System.out.println(printed); System.out.println(text); try { lines.add(new LineJava("late.pdf", 1, 1)); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("the copied list is read-only: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } }

try.expect: Both print [flyer.pdf, menu.pdf, cover-sheet.pdf], {flyer.pdf=250, menu.pdf=320, cover-sheet.pdf=1}, pages to print=571 and a line saying the list is read-only. Inside the block, this is the standard library's own list builder class (it prints ListBuilder), not an ArrayList: that's how the result can become read-only without a copy. With the if first, size is 0, so no cover sheet is added.

sections.h: @DslMarker: each section of the form offers only its own boxes
sections.html:
The demo's order form shows the trap best. It has two sections that look alike, the customer and the delivery address. Both take a name and a phone number, so both use one builder class, ContactBuilder. Around them sits OrderFormBuilder, which holds the number of copies and offers the customer { } and deliverTo { } blocks.

Inside customer { }, two receivers are in scope: the ContactBuilder for the customer, and the OrderFormBuilder around it. For a call that names no receiver, Kotlin tries each receiver in turn, nearest first. So a deliverTo { } written by mistake inside customer { } compiles. ContactBuilder has no deliverTo, and the compiler, always eager to help, finds one on the outer builder and calls that.

On paper, that would be a form where any box missing from your section gets written into the section underneath. The demo's wrong move does exactly that. Without a marker, it compiles, runs, and fails with IllegalArgumentException: phone required for 'oops': the misplaced line built a second, half-filled delivery address. The exception is luck. On a form without a required phone number, the shop would deliver to "oops".

@DslMarker closes the hole. It is an annotation, a label in the source that tools can read, and you put it on an annotation class of your own. Then you put your annotation on every builder class. From then on, inside a block, only the nearest marked receiver is implicit. Each section offers only its own boxes:

Java
// Java needs no marker: each lambda names its builder, so reaching the outer one takes `f.`
DslMarkerDemoKt.orderForm("ord-17", f -> {
    f.customer(c -> {
        c.setName("Corner Bakery");
        c.setPhone("555-0142");
        f.setCopies(250);                  // deliberate, and visible in review
        return Unit.INSTANCE;
    });
    f.deliverTo(c -> { c.setName("Back door"); c.setPhone("555-0143"); return Unit.INSTANCE; });
    return Unit.INSTANCE;
});
Kotlin
@DslMarker
@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPE)
annotation class FormDsl

@FormDsl class ContactBuilder { /* name, phone, build() */ }
@FormDsl class OrderFormBuilder(private val id: String) { /* copies, customer { }, deliverTo { } */ }

orderForm("ord-18") {
    customer {
        name = "Corner Bakery"
        deliverTo { name = "oops" }        // error: cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver
        this@orderForm.copies = 250        // an explicit label still works
    }
}

The full message is 'fun deliverTo(block: ContactBuilder.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. A box from the outer section fails the same way: copies = 5 inside customer { } gets 'var copies: Int' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver.

You can still reach the outer section on purpose, by naming it. this@orderForm is a labeled this: it names the receiver of the lambda passed to orderForm, and nobody types it by accident. On the paper form, it's writing "order section, copies: 250" in full.

Without a marker, a missing name falls through to the outer builder. Mark every builder class.

The rules are narrow, so learn them exactly. A marker counts only where it marks a type. That can be a builder class, or a common superclass of all the builders, which is enough for a DSL with twenty of them. It can be the receiver type of a function type (the TYPE target, as in @FormDsl ContactBuilder.() -> Unit). Or it can be a type alias, a second name for a type. Every builder needs it. Leave ContactBuilder unmarked, and the wrong move compiles again.

On a function, the marker does nothing. If your annotation's @Target allows functions, Kotlin 2.4.21 warns applying DSL marker annotation 'FormDsl' to target 'member function' has no effect. With @Target(CLASS, TYPE), as here, it refuses outright: this annotation is not applicable to target 'member function'. Extension functions on a marked builder still work inside its block, because they resolve against the nearest receiver.

The paper picture breaks in your favor here. A clerk finds a misfiled box after the form is handed in. The compiler finds it before the program ever runs.

The DSL now catches misplaced words in Kotlin. Java callers never had that problem, but they have one of their own.

video.title: A lambda with receiver runs inside its builder; a bare call goes to the nearest receiver that has it, and @DslMarker stops it there

sections.h: Calling the DSL from Java, and what became of context receivers
sections.html:
A Kotlin DSL works from Java, though it isn't pretty. Every Builder.() -> Unit parameter is a Function1<Builder, Unit>, so a Java caller writes b -> { b.cover(4); ...; return Unit.INSTANCE; }. The lab's OrderFromJavaTest does just that.

If Java callers matter to you, add a thin second entry point that takes a java.util.function.Consumer, Java's own interface for a block that takes one value and returns nothing. Give it a name of its own, so Kotlin callers never have to choose between two kinds of lambda:

Java
Booklet menu = PrintOrderKt.printBookletJava("menu", b -> {
    b.cover(4);
    b.pages("dishes", 8);               // a void lambda: no Unit.INSTANCE
});
Kotlin
fun printBookletJava(title: String, block: Consumer<BookletBuilder>): Booklet =
    printBooklet(title) { block.accept(this) }    // `this` is the BookletBuilder

@DslMarker means nothing to Java, and Java doesn't need it. A Java lambda names its parameter, b or c, so reaching an outer builder always means typing its name. The demo's Java twin writes f.setCopies(250) inside the address block, on purpose and in plain sight.

DSLs were also the main reason for an experiment you'll still meet in older code and blog posts: context receivers. A context receiver let a function demand a receiver from its surroundings, as in context(Logbook) fun hello(), so a DSL word could only be used inside the right block. Kotlin 1.6.20 shipped them as a prototype behind a compiler flag (an option you pass to the compiler), -Xcontext-receivers, and warned that the result could not be used in production code. Kotlin 2.2.0 replaced them with a new design, context parameters, as a preview. Kotlin 2.3.20 removed the old one: "Experimental context receivers are no longer supported and are replaced by context parameters."

Kotlin 2.4.21 tells you so when it meets the old syntax. You get context parameters must be named. Use '_' to declare an anonymous context parameter., then unresolved reference 'write', because a context parameter is not a receiver inside the body. The old flag fails on its own, with experimental context receivers are superseded by context parameters. Remove the '-Xcontext-receivers' compiler argument and migrate to the new syntax. When you see either message, the next lesson has the fix: context parameters, stable since Kotlin 2.4.0.

That leaves the limit of today's tool. A DSL and its marker check where a word is written, and only in Kotlin. Rules between values, such as the multiple of 4, still run in build() when the program runs, and Java callers get no marker at all.

A check before you move on: a Java caller passes b -> { b.cover(4); b.pages("dishes", 8); } to printBooklet, with no return at the end. Predict what javac says, and why the same lambda is fine for printBookletJava. (The answer follows from the two interfaces: Function1.invoke returns a value, and Consumer.accept returns void.)

compare.title: A booklet builder: Java Consumer vs Kotlin lambda with receiver

java.title: Booklets.java
java.html: public final class Booklets { public static Booklet booklet(String title, Consumer<BookletBuilder> block) { BookletBuilder b = new BookletBuilder(title); block.accept(b); // the builder arrives as a parameter return b.build(); } } Booklet menu = Booklets.booklet("menu", b -> { b.setNote("staple on the fold"); b.cover(4); b.pages("starters", 4); b.pages("mains", 8); });

kotlin.title: Booklets.kt
kotlin.html: fun printBooklet(title: String, block: BookletBuilder.() -> Unit): Booklet = BookletBuilder(title).apply(block).build() // the builder is `this` inside block val menu = printBooklet("menu") { note = "staple on the fold" cover(4) pages("starters", 4) pages("mains", 8) }

compare.note: Both compile to the same thing: a function object that receives the builder. On the JVM, Kotlin's BookletBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<BookletBuilder, Unit>, and Java's Consumer<BookletBuilder> plays the same role. The difference lives only in the source. Kotlin makes the builder this, so the block reads like the booklet it describes, and nested blocks need @DslMarker to stop calls from reaching outer builders by accident. Java names the parameter on every line, which is noisier but can never send a call to the wrong builder.

worked.title: Add a word to the booklet DSL with an extension function

steps.say: Concert programmes at the shop all have the same shape: a 4-page card cover, the content, then blank pages so the total folds. Written out each time, the padding sum gets copied by hand, and one day it gets copied wrong.
steps.code: Booklets.booklet("concert", b -> { b.cover(4); b.pages("programme", 10); b.pages("blank", 2); // 4 + 10 + 2 = 16, worked out by hand });

alt.html: printBooklet("concert") { cover(4) pages("programme", 10) pages("blank", 2) // 4 + 10 + 2 = 16, worked out by hand }

steps.say: Write an extension function on the builder. It works even when BookletBuilder lives in a library you can't edit, and inside a block it reads like a word the builder always had.
steps.code: fun BookletBuilder.folded(name: String, contentPages: Int) { // 1. the cover and the content, as before cover(4) pages(name, contentPages) // 2. the padding, worked out once, in one place val blanks = (4 - contentPages % 4) % 4 if (blanks > 0) pages("blank", blanks) } printBooklet("concert") { folded("programme", 10) }

alt.html: // Java's version is a static helper that takes the builder as its first parameter, // which is exactly what the Kotlin extension compiles to static void folded(BookletBuilder b, String name, int contentPages) { b.cover(4); b.pages(name, contentPages); int blanks = (4 - contentPages % 4) % 4; if (blanks > 0) b.pages("blank", blanks); }

steps.say: Check where it can be called. Inside booklet { } it resolves against the nearest receiver, the BookletBuilder. Directly inside printOrder { } it doesn't compile, so nobody can pad an order instead of a booklet.
steps.code: printOrder("ord-17") { booklet("programme") { folded("concert", 10) } // fine folded("recital", 6) // error: candidate 'fun BookletBuilder.folded(name: String, contentPages: Int): Unit' is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch. }

alt.html: PrintOrderKt.printOrder("ord-17", o -> { o.booklet("programme", b -> { folded(b, "concert", 10); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); // fine // folded(o, "recital", 6); // error: incompatible types: OrderBuilder cannot be converted to BookletBuilder return Unit.INSTANCE; });

steps.say: Run it: the programme has a 4-page cover, 10 pages of content and 2 blank pages, 16 in all, and build() accepts it because 16 folds. Whether blank pages go at the end or just before the back cover is a shop rule, and it now lives in one function you can test.

lab.title: A booklet-order DSL
steps: An order holds booklets, and each booklet holds parts: a cover on card and pages of plain paper. Run the tests. All seven fail.
In BookletBuilder, keep the parts in a private list, and write cover and pages so they reject a page count of 0 or less (TODO 1).
Write build() (TODO 2): at least two parts, a total that is a multiple of 4, and a copy of the list in the result.
Write OrderBuilder (TODO 3) and the two entry functions (TODO 4). Each is one or two lines once BookletBuilder works.

Before adding the marker, write a scratch function with booklet("b2") { ... } inside another booklet { } of an order. It compiles, and b2 even lands in the order ahead of the booklet you were writing. Then put @OrderDsl on both builders (TODO 5) and read the error.
Run until all seven pass, including OrderFromJavaTest, which builds a booklet from Java with a Function1.
hints: A private helper add(name, paper, pages) that calls require(pages > 0) { ... } and then parts += Part(name, paper, pages) keeps cover and pages to one line each.
parts.sumOf { it.pages } gives the total, and total % 4 == 0 says whether it folds.
parts.toList() makes the copy, so later calls on the builder can't change a booklet you already built.
In OrderBuilder.booklet, check for a duplicate title before you build: require(booklets.none { it.title == title }) { ... }.
lab.done: All seven tests in OrderDslTest and OrderFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write a tiny CSV-line DSL from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write csvLine { field("job_7"); field(250); field("A4") } returning "job_7,250,A4": a builder class with field(value: Any) and an entry function that takes a lambda with receiver. Then write the Java version with a Consumer. Which line in the Kotlin version makes the builder this?

answer.html: class CsvLine { private val fields = mutableListOf<String>() fun field(value: Any) { fields += value.toString() } fun build(): String = fields.joinToString(",") } // the parameter type CsvLine.() -> Unit is what makes the builder `this` inside the braces fun csvLine(block: CsvLine.() -> Unit): String = CsvLine().apply(block).build() val line = csvLine { field("job_7"); field(250); field("A4") } // job_7,250,A4

alt.title: CsvLine.java
alt.html: final class CsvLine { private final List<String> fields = new ArrayList<>(); void field(Object value) { fields.add(String.valueOf(value)); } String build() { return String.join(",", fields); } static String csvLine(Consumer<CsvLine> block) { CsvLine b = new CsvLine(); block.accept(b); // the builder is a parameter, not `this` return b.build(); } } String line = CsvLine.csvLine(b -> { b.field("job_7"); b.field(250); b.field("A4"); });

recap: A.() -> B is a function type with a receiver: inside the lambda, the A is this. On the JVM it's a Function1<A, B>, interchangeable with (A) -> B.
A DSL is builder classes plus entry functions of the form Builder().apply(block).build(). No library is needed, and buildList, buildMap and buildString come with the standard library.
Check one value at the call that passes it, and rules between values in build(), the one place that sees them all.
@DslMarker on every builder class makes only the nearest receiver implicit; reach an outer one with this@label. On a function, a marker does nothing.
Java calls a DSL with Function1 lambdas that return Unit.INSTANCE, or through a Consumer entry point with its own name. Context receivers, the old DSL experiment, are gone since Kotlin 2.3.20.
The limit: the marker checks only where a word is written, and only in Kotlin. Rules between values still fail at run time, in build().

explain.prompt: A teammate's test fills in an order form with deliverTo { } accidentally written inside customer { }, and it compiled. Explain why it compiled, and what @DslMarker changes.
explain.answer: Inside customer { } there are two implicit receivers: the ContactBuilder the block was given, and the OrderFormBuilder from the orderForm { } block around it. When Kotlin sees a call that names no receiver, it tries each receiver in scope, nearest first. ContactBuilder has no deliverTo, so the compiler found deliverTo on the outer builder and called that, which built a second address in the wrong place. Nothing in the types was wrong, so it compiled. @DslMarker is a rule about those receivers: if the builder classes carry the same marker annotation, only the nearest marked receiver is implicit inside a block. The misplaced deliverTo { } becomes a compile error that says it can't be called with an implicit receiver. If you really mean the outer builder, you name it with this@orderForm, which nobody writes by accident. The marker has to be on every builder class; leaving one out, or putting it on the functions, does nothing.

deeper.html:
Context parameters, the subject of the next lesson, meet implicit receivers in one tricky case, and Kotlin 2.4.21 is strict about it. Here a with block makes one printer the receiver, and a context(...) block brings a second printer into scope as a context value:

Java
// No Java twin: Java has neither receivers nor context parameters.
// The nearest idea is two parameters of the same type, where you must pick one by name.
record Printer(String name) {}

static void beep(Printer printer) { System.out.println("beep from " + printer.name()); }
Kotlin
class Printer(val name: String) { fun beep() = println("beep from $name") }

with(Printer("laser-1")) {
    context(Printer("laser-2")) {
        beep()   // which printer?
    }
}

A bare beep() would go to the receiver, laser-1, which is probably not what the author meant. Kotlin 2.4.21 reports an error: call to 'fun beep(): Unit' defined in 'Printer' uses an implicit receiver shadowed by a context parameter. Make the receiver explicit using 'this' or 'contextOf<Printer>()'. The type-safe builders page calls this a warning. The compiler you run is what counts, and here it is stricter than the page. The design document for context parameters, KEEP-0367, uses the same shape of example with a cow that moos.

A second detail: the TYPE target on the marker lets you mark one block without marking the class, as in fun customer(block: @FormDsl ContactBuilder.() -> Unit). That helps when the builder comes from a library you can't annotate. And when you design a DSL for others, keep each builder's list of members short. The IDE offers every public member inside the block, and every one of them is a word someone will eventually use in the wrong place.
